flashcards.q: What is the Bar Raiser and what does that mean for your prep?
flashcards.a: A trained interviewer pulled from a different team than the hiring one, with VETO power over the decision, whose job is keeping the bar consistent by probing past the rehearsed layer of your answer. It means depth per story matters more than story count, and every number you cite gets drilled.

flashcards.q: How is an Amazon loop structured, and how many LP questions should you expect?
flashcards.a: Four to five back-to-back interviews, each interviewer assigned two to three specific Leadership Principles so the panel collectively covers all 16, meaning roughly 12-15 LP questions in a day. Every round also has a technical component. At Principal level, reported at seven to eight rounds.

flashcards.q: Which four LPs cluster heaviest in engineering loops in practice?
flashcards.a: Dive Deep, Deliver Results, Invent and Simplify, Bias for Action. Prepare two stories each for these four rather than one story each for all sixteen.

flashcards.q: What does Amazon's own Principal Engineering tenets material say about Deliver Results, and what does it expect instead?
flashcards.a: Deliver Results is described as a LOW BAR for a Principal Engineer. Expected instead: lasting impact that echoes through the technology, product and company; bringing clarity to complexity and framing problems in customer and business context; staying hands-on and leading by example; educating the organisation about trends and approaches.

flashcards.q: Which two Amazon LPs are gaps in this resume, and what must be done?
flashcards.a: Hire and Develop the Best, and Strive to be Earth's Best Employer. Both are people-facing and neither appears on the resume. At Principal level the first will almost certainly be asked. Write one real story each: onboarding someone, raising the review bar, a runbook that stopped a recurring page, changing the on-call rotation, or running interviews.

flashcards.q: What is Google's decisive hiring mechanism, and its single most actionable consequence?
flashcards.a: A hiring committee of senior Googlers who never interviewed you and do not know the hiring team, scoring the written evidence packet. Consequence: anything that does not survive transcription does not count. '54,486 skills across 22 locales resolved through a tiered cascade' survives; 'large-scale multilingual skill system' does not.

flashcards.q: Name Google's four scored attributes and what GCA actually measures.
flashcards.a: Role-Related Knowledge, General Cognitive Ability, Leadership, Googleyness. GCA measures whether your reasoning is structured and adaptive, not whether you reached the right answer, which is why announcing your reasoning structure out loud is itself evidence.

flashcards.q: What does Googleyness explicitly include, and how must it be demonstrated?
flashcards.a: Intellectual humility, comfort with ambiguity, bias to action, collaboration. It must be shown through described BEHAVIOUR, not stated values: noticing that a disagreement was blocking progress and scheduling one-on-ones counts; 'I value collaboration' does not.

flashcards.q: What is the Meta E6 onsite structure in 2026, and what is new?
flashcards.a: One standard coding round, one AI-ASSISTED coding round, one architecture round, one design round, one behavioural round, plus a Leadership Assessment interview before the onsite that replaces the phone screen at this level and is roughly half behavioural and half coding. The AI-assisted round is the notable change; the stated intent is judging whether you can direct work including machine-generated work.

flashcards.q: What does Meta's behavioural round score, and what is the E6 scope bar?
flashcards.a: The 'Jedi' round scores ownership, collaboration, conflict, execution under ambiguity, and learning from mistakes. E6 bar: a disagreement story must involve TWO OR MORE TEAMS on the direction of a large project, and an impact story must have large impact on the ORG, not the team. Single-team stories read as E5.

flashcards.q: What is Microsoft's 'As Appropriate' round and how do you read it?
flashcards.a: The final round, usually run by a Principal Engineering Manager or Partner-level leader, tailored to how you performed earlier; interviewers sync notes first. Relaxed and mostly pitching the team means sell mode and the earlier rounds went well. Aggressively testing technical gaps means you are borderline. Actionable: track your own weakest answer between rounds and prepare the second pass.

flashcards.q: Why is Microsoft the best rubric fit for this resume?
flashcards.a: Microsoft's world is enterprise realities: multi-tenancy, compliance, global readiness, security, backward compatibility, migration of installed customers. That maps directly onto the 22-locale hardening, the cross-tenant authorization fix, the multi-tenant provisioning ingestion, and the Java-to-Python migration with its cutover strategy. Growth mindset is also a real rubric item, so a calibrated answer is safer than a bold one.

flashcards.q: What is distinctive about a Netflix loop, and what must you practise?
flashcards.a: Conversational, domain-specific, frequently NO shared whiteboard (multiple candidates report completing system design with no diagramming tool), roughly seven interviews, keeper-test framing with the written culture memo as the actual rubric. Practise verbal architecture: number the components, state direction explicitly, name them once and reuse the names.

flashcards.q: How does Netflix's rubric change how you tell a self-critical story?
flashcards.a: Candour is scored positively, including toward the interviewer, so 'eight services was too many and here's what I'd do instead' lands better at Netflix than anywhere else. Expect fewer prompts: silence is the absence of scaffolding, not disapproval. Agreeing with everything reads as low talent density.

flashcards.q: What is the decisive round at OpenAI, and what is the screen format?
flashcards.a: A PAID 48-hour work trial graded on shipping speed, code quality, design choices and how you write tests. The technical screen uses a progressive GATE format where one problem gets harder across roughly four stages and most candidates report needing to clear at least two. Process varies by team, and the AI-tool policy varies by team too (research generally AI-prohibited).

flashcards.q: What is the Anthropic engineering loop and what is the distinctive coding format?
flashcards.a: Five stages over roughly four to six weeks for engineering: recruiter screen, 60-minute technical phone screen with one medium-hard problem, take-home, onsite. The coding round is writing code fast to a spec then REFACTORING quickly as constraints are added per stage, in a four-level assessment. The bar for written reasoning is high; culture fit means taking safety seriously without being a doomer.

flashcards.q: Which stories lead at an AI lab, and which metrics must you swap out?
flashcards.a: Lead with vLLM serving (continuous batching, PagedAttention, KV-cache sizing, instance benchmarking), A2A plus FastMCP with the multi-agent test stated, async LLM rate limiting under distributed concurrency, and the golden baseline for a non-deterministic system. Swap product metrics (~25% engagement) for systems metrics: throughput, cost per million tokens, p99, index size, KV-cache-bound concurrency.

flashcards.q: What are the three weaknesses of this profile at an AI lab?
flashcards.a: 1) The evaluation story is thinner than the systems story: RAGAS and DeepEval are listed but not shown producing a decision. 2) No dollar cost model or break-even for the self-hosting decision, and they will ask. 3) No public artifact: a write-up of the OOM fix or the KV-cache sizing work, or a published MCP server, would materially help and costs a weekend.

flashcards.q: What is the single axis that explains most variation between these six companies?
flashcards.a: Where the hiring decision is made and what protects it from being wrong. Amazon: panel with an outside Bar Raiser holding veto. Google: a committee who never met you reading a written packet. Meta: a calibrated panel where speed is itself signal. Microsoft: hiring manager plus an AA round targeting your gaps. Netflix: manager under keeper-test norms with the culture memo as rubric. AI labs: a graded work trial.

flashcards.q: What is the core reframing principle across companies?
flashcards.a: The same story needs four or five different FRAMINGS, not four or five different stories. Amazon leads with the customer; Google leads with quotable specifics; Meta compresses and ends on self-critique; Microsoft leads into domain depth; Netflix opens with candour; AI labs lead with ship velocity and cost.

flashcards.q: What should you always ask the recruiter, and why?
flashcards.a: What the rounds actually are. Published loop structures vary by team, level, region and recruiter, so the reported process is frequently wrong for your specific loop. Recruiters usually tell you, and asking is a positive signal rather than a neutral one.
